mcqs.question: What specifically does dropout prevent units in a layer from doing?
options: Learning any features at all
Receiving gradients during backpropagation
Using more than one activation function
Co-adapting — relying on a narrow, brittle combination of specific other units
mcqs.explanation: By randomly zeroing different units each step, dropout stops units from depending on always having the same specific neighbors active, which forces more robust, individually useful features. Units still learn and still receive gradients — dropout doesn't disable learning, it changes what gets learned.

mcqs.question: During training, validation loss bottoms out at epoch 12 and starts rising afterward while training loss keeps falling. What does early stopping do here?
options: Stops training and keeps the checkpoint from around epoch 12, before validation loss started rising
Continues training to the final epoch, then keeps the last checkpoint
Restarts training from scratch with a different architecture
Ignores validation loss entirely and only tracks training loss
mcqs.explanation: Early stopping tracks validation loss specifically because it's the signal for when the model starts overfitting training-set noise; it keeps the best checkpoint (around epoch 12 here) rather than a later, more-overfit one. Training loss alone can't reveal overfitting since it keeps improving even as generalization worsens.

mcqs.question: A deployed model with dropout layers gives a different prediction for the identical input on two separate API calls. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model wasn't trained long enough
Dropout was left active at inference instead of being disabled
The learning rate was too high during training
The input wasn't normalized correctly
mcqs.explanation: Dropout randomly zeroes units on each forward pass; if it's still active at inference (model not switched to eval mode), identical inputs will produce different outputs across calls, since a different random set of units gets dropped each time. The other options would cause consistent but poor predictions, not non-determinism.

mcqs.question: What problem does label smoothing address that hard one-hot targets create during training?
options: Hard targets make the loss function impossible to differentiate

Hard one-hot targets push the network toward extreme, overconfident logits since cross-entropy keeps rewarding higher confidence on the correct class; smoothing softens the target so confidence isn't pushed to the extreme
Hard targets prevent the model from ever reaching 90% accuracy
Hard targets only cause problems in regression tasks, not classification
mcqs.explanation: Cross-entropy against a one-hot target has no upper bound on how much it rewards pushing confidence toward 100%, driving overconfident logits; label smoothing removes that incentive by softening the target itself. Cross-entropy remains fully differentiable with hard targets, hard targets don't cap achievable accuracy, and this is a classification-specific concern tied to one-hot targets.

mcqs.question: A team switches from Adam with an L2 penalty to AdamW but keeps the exact same weight-decay numeric value. What's the risk?
options: There is no risk, since weight decay behaves identically in both cases
AdamW will fail to run at all with a value tuned for Adam

Because AdamW applies decay decoupled from the adaptive per-parameter scaling while Adam+L2 entangles the two, the same numeric value produces a different effective regularization strength, potentially too weak or too strong
AdamW ignores the weight-decay parameter entirely
mcqs.explanation: The mechanism differs between the two: Adam+L2's penalty interacts with the adaptive scaling, while AdamW's decoupled decay doesn't, so an unchanged numeric value doesn't produce equivalent regularization strength in both — it needs re-tuning. AdamW runs fine with such a value (it just may be miscalibrated), and it certainly doesn't ignore the parameter.
